Jesus continues preaching (verse 1)

Our divine Redeemer never grew tired of his work of love.

We should likewise refuse to grow weary of doing good, knowing that in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.

Jesus answers John the Baptist's disciples (verses 2–6)

There are two possible explanations for John's message.

Some believe he sent his disciples because he himself desired reassurance. Genuine faith can still be mixed with unbelief, and temptation may temporarily lead even good people to question important truths.

Yet Henry hopes John's faith did not fail in this matter and that he wanted only to have it strengthened and confirmed.

Others believe John sent them for the disciples' own benefit, so that Jesus would assure them directly.

Christ pointed them toward what they had heard and seen.

His merciful works, particularly toward poor people, identified him as the One bringing the tender mercies of God into the world.

When what people hear and see is compared carefully with Scripture, it points toward the way of salvation.

Prejudice is difficult to overcome, but allowing it to rule is dangerous.

Faith that continues despite prejudice and opposition will ultimately bring greater praise, honor and glory.

Jesus honors John the Baptist (verses 7–15)

Jesus praised John not simply to honor him but to help the listeners.

Everyone who hears God's word will have to give an account of what they did with it.

The end of a sermon is not the end of our responsibility; in an important sense, it is when the real work begins.

John practiced serious self-denial and was detached from luxury, outward pomp and sensual pleasure.

Our conduct and appearance should be consistent with our calling and situation.

John was great and good, but not perfect.

In that sense he fell short of believers already glorified in heaven.

Even the least of them knows, loves and praises God more fully than the greatest saint in this world.

But Henry judges that “the kingdom of heaven” in this passage refers more especially to the kingdom of grace, the gospel age in its power and purity.

We should be thankful for living amid the advantages of its light and love.

John's ministry stirred many people, who became his disciples.

People previously thought unlikely to have any interest in God's kingdom now strove earnestly to enter it, seeming almost like unexpected intruders.

This illustrates the urgency and zeal required of us all.

Self must be denied. Our hearts, habits of mind and fundamental dispositions must change.

Those who truly desire God's great salvation will receive it on the terms he sets, refusing to let go until they obtain his blessing.

Divine things concern everyone.

God requires that people use the abilities he gives them properly.

Many remain ignorant because they refuse to learn.

Jesus exposes a stubborn generation (verses 16–24)

Jesus reproved the self-important scribes and Pharisees.

Their behavior resembled children who refuse to join their companions' games and complain no matter how others try to please them.

Worldly people often produce petty criticisms of everyone, however good and holy the person may be.

Their objections reveal malice more than wisdom.

John's austere life displeased them, and Jesus' fellowship with people displeased them too.

Christ, completely holy and separate from sin, was accused of joining in sinners' wrongdoing.

Even spotless innocence cannot always protect a person from slander.

Jesus knew that many Jewish hearers had become more hardened against his miracles and teaching than people in Tyre and Sidon would have been.

Their judgment would therefore be more serious.

God possesses almighty power but never punishes anyone beyond what is deserved, nor withholds truth from people who genuinely long to know it.

Jesus invites the weary to find rest (verses 25–30)

Children should be grateful.

When we approach God as Father, we must also remember that he is Lord of heaven and earth.

We should come with reverence before the sovereign Ruler of all and with confidence that he can protect us from evil and give us what is good.

Jesus made the extraordinary declaration that the Father had entrusted all power, authority and judgment into his hands.

Every revelation of the Father's will and love since Adam sinned has come to us through Christ.

The Savior invites everyone who labors and is heavily burdened to come to him.

In different senses, all human beings are burdened.

Some wear themselves out pursuing wealth, position and honor.

Others exhaust themselves chasing pleasure.

People enslaved to Satan and their own desires endure the harshest bondage.

Others labor uselessly trying to establish their own righteousness before God.

Convinced sinners feel guilt and dread. Tempted and suffering believers also carry real burdens.

Christ invites them all to come to him for rest for their souls.

He himself issues this invitation.

We come when, aware of guilt and misery, believing his love and power to help, we seek him earnestly through prayer.

It is both our duty and our highest interest to come.

The gospel's summons is generous: Whoever desires may come.

All who come this way receive rest as Christ's free gift, finding peace and comfort in the heart.

But we must take his yoke and willingly submit to his authority.

We must learn from him both how to obey and how to receive comfort.

He accepts willing service even when the service is imperfect.

His commands are holy, just and good.

They do require self-denial and can bring difficulty, yet his grace provides inward joy and peace even in this life.

His yoke is, as Henry puts it, lined with love.

The help Christ supplies is so powerful, his encouragements so suitable and his consolations so strong that obedience becomes pleasant.

The path of duty is the path of rest.

We may confidently stake our souls on the truths he teaches.

Why then would weary sinners seek rest elsewhere?

Let us come to Christ daily for deliverance from wrath and guilt, from sin and Satan, and from our worries, fears and sorrows.

Forced, unwilling obedience is a heavy burden rather than a light yoke.

It is useless to approach Jesus with our lips while keeping our hearts far from him.

Come to him and receive rest for your souls.

Verse 1
Our Divine Redeemer never was weary of his labour of love; and we should not be weary of well-doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
[Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6]
Verses 2-6
Some think that John sent this inquiry for his own satisfaction. Where there is true faith, yet there may be a mixture of unbelief. The remaining unbelief of good men may sometimes, in an hour of temptation; call in question the most important truths. But we hope that John's faith did not fail in this matter, and that he only desired to have it strengthened and confirmed. Others think that John sent his disciples to Christ for their satisfaction. Christ points them to what they heard and saw. Christ's gracious condescensions and compassions to the poor, show that it was he that should bring to the world the tender mercies of our God. Those things which men see and hear, if compared with the Scriptures, direct in what way salvation is to be found. It is difficult to conquer prejudices, and dangerous not to conquer them; but those who believe in Christ, their faith will be found so much the more to praise, and honour, and glory.
[Matt.11.7-Matt.11.15]
Verses 7-15
What Christ said concerning John, was not only for his praise, but for the people's profit. Those who attend on the word will be called to give an account of their improvements. Do we think when the sermon is done, the care is over? No, then the greatest of the care begins. John was a self-denying man, dead to all the pomps of the world and the pleasures of sense. It becomes people, in all their appearances, to be consistent with their character and their situation. John was a great and good man, yet not perfect; therefore he came short of glorified saints. The least in heaven knows more, loves more, and does more in praising God, and receives more from him, than the greatest in this world. But by the kingdom of heaven here, is rather to be understood the kingdom of grace, the gospel dispensation in its power and purity. What reason we have to be thankful that our lot is cast in the days of the kingdom of heaven, under such advantages of light and love! Multitudes were wrought upon by the ministry of John, and became his disciples. And those strove for a place in this kingdom, that one would think had no right nor title to it, and so seemed to be intruders. It shows us what fervency and zeal are required of all. Self must be denied; the bent, the frame and temper of the mind must be altered. Those who will have an interest in the great salvation, will have it upon any terms, and not think them hard, nor quit their hold without a blessing. The things of God are of great and common concern. God requires no more from us than the right use of the faculties he has given us. People are ignorant, because they will not learn.
[Matt.11.16-Matt.11.24]
Verses 16-24
Christ reflects on the scribes and Pharisees, who had a proud conceit of themselves. He likens their behaviour to children's play, who being out of temper without reason, quarrel with all the attempts of their fellows to please them, or to get them to join in the plays for which they used to assemble. The cavils of worldly men are often very trifling and show great malice. Something they have to urge against every one, however excellent and holy. Christ, who was undefiled, and separate from sinners, is here represented as in league with them, and polluted by them. The most unspotted innocence will not always be a defence against reproach. Christ knew that the hearts of the Jews were more bitter and hardened against his miracles and doctrines, than those of Tyre and Sidon would have been; therefore their condemnation would be the greater. The Lord exercises his almighty power, yet he punishes none more than they deserve, and never withholds the knowledge of the truth from those who long after it.
[Matt.11.25-Matt.11.30]
Verses 25-30
It becomes children to be grateful. When we come to God as a Father, we must remember that he is Lord of heaven and earth, which obliges us to come to him with reverence as to the sovereign Lord of all; yet with confidence, as one able to defend us from evil, and to supply us with all good. Our blessed Lord added a remarkable declaration, that the Father had delivered into his hands all power, authority, and judgment. We are indebted to Christ for all the revelation we have of God the Father's will and love, ever since Adam sinned. Our Saviour has invited all that labour and are heavy-laden, to come unto him. In some senses all men are so. Worldly men burden themselves with fruitless cares for wealth and honours; the gay and the sensual labour in pursuit of pleasures; the slave of Satan and his own lusts, is the merest drudge on earth. Those who labour to establish their own righteousness also labour in vain. The convinced sinner is heavy-laden with guilt and terror; and the tempted and afflicted believer has labours and burdens. Christ invites all to come to him for rest to their souls. He alone gives this invitation; men come to him, when, feeling their guilt and misery, and believing his love and power to help, they seek him in fervent prayer. Thus it is the duty and interest of weary and heavy-laden sinners, to come to Jesus Christ. This is the gospel call; Whoever will, let him come. All who thus come will receive rest as Christ's gift, and obtain peace and comfort in their hearts. But in coming to him they must take his yoke, and submit to his authority. They must learn of him all things, as to their comfort and obedience. He accepts the willing servant, however imperfect the services. Here we may find rest for our souls, and here only. Nor need we fear his yoke. His commandments are holy, just, and good. It requires self-denial, and exposes to difficulties, but this is abundantly repaid, even in this world, by inward peace and joy. It is a yoke that is lined with love. So powerful are the assistances he gives us, so suitable the encouragements, and so strong the consolations to be found in the way of duty, that we may truly say, it is a yoke of pleasantness. The way of duty is the way of rest. The truths Christ teaches are such as we may venture our souls upon. Such is the Redeemer's mercy; and why should the labouring and burdened sinner seek for rest from any other quarter? Let us come to him daily, for deliverance from wrath and guilt, from sin and Satan, from all our cares, fears, and sorrows. But forced obedience, far from being easy and light, is a heavy burden. In vain do we draw near to Jesus with our lips, while the heart is far from him. Then come to Jesus to find rest for your souls.

The disciples gather grain on the Sabbath (verses 1–8)

When the disciples plucked grain, they acted within God's law (Deuteronomy 23:25). They had little food and were content with that modest provision.

The Pharisees did not object because the grain belonged to another person; they objected because it was the Sabbath.

Christ came to free his followers from the Pharisees' unscriptural human rules, not merely their moral corruption, and he defended what the disciples did.

The strongest person's desires must not be indulged at the expense of the weakest person's genuine needs.

Work that is necessary is lawful on the Sabbath. The day's rest should promote, not prevent, worship.

Reasonable food and care for health are proper. But forcing servants to stay home and turning a household into a scene of haste and disorder in order to prepare an indulgent feast for visitors is a very different matter.

Henry explicitly reproves such conduct, even among people who profess faith.

The Sabbath was instituted for human good (Deuteronomy 5:14). No law should be interpreted in a way that defeats its own purpose.

Christ is Lord of the Sabbath. Both the day and the appropriate work of that day belong to him.

Jesus heals a withered hand (verses 9–13)

Works of mercy are lawful and fitting on the Lord's day.

There are useful acts beyond formal worship: visiting the sick, feeding the poor, helping those needing urgent assistance and teaching young people to care for their souls.

Such things must come from love and generosity, with humility and self-denial, and are acceptable to God (Genesis 4:7, as cited in this secondary witness).

As with other miracles, this healing also has a spiritual meaning.

By nature our hands are spiritually withered; we cannot produce good works through our own power.

Christ alone gives life to the dead soul.

He works within us both the desire and the ability to obey.

His command comes with the promise of grace through his word.

The Pharisees plot against Jesus (verses 14–21)

The Pharisees looked for a charge that would allow them to put Jesus to death.

Knowing their plan and that his appointed time had not yet come, Christ withdrew.

His character and conduct fulfilled the prophet's description with extraordinary exactness.

We may confidently entrust ourselves to so kind and faithful a Friend.

He does not break the bruised reed but strengthens it.

He does not extinguish the weakly smoking wick but encourages its flame.

Let us abandon quarrelsome and angry argument and receive one another as Christ has received us.

Encouraged by his gentleness, let us pray that his Spirit will rest upon us and help us follow his example.

Jesus delivers a man oppressed by a demon (verses 22–30)

A soul held captive by Satan is spiritually blind to God's truth and unable to speak properly in prayer.

Through unbelief the devil closes the eyes; through temptation he keeps the lips from praying.

The more people admired Christ's miracle, the more urgently the Pharisees tried to discredit him.

But if Satan were helping Jesus to expel demons, his own kingdom would be fighting itself and could not stand.

And if the Pharisees claimed Jesus acted through the devil's prince, they had no valid reason to say their own followers' exorcisms used a different power.

There are two great opposed interests in the world.

Where the Holy Spirit casts out evil through conversion, leading sinners to faith and obedience, God's kingdom has come.

Anyone who refuses to welcome or assist this gracious change opposes Christ.

Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (verses 31 and 32)

Jesus first gives a gracious assurance that all kinds of sin may be pardoned on gospel terms.

He also teaches his followers to be willing to forgive insulting words directed against themselves.

Humble, conscientious believers sometimes fear that they have committed the unforgivable sin.

Yet people who have approached that sin most closely seldom feel troubled about it.

People who sincerely repent and believe the gospel have not committed the unpardonable sin.

Repentance and faith are special gifts of God. He would not give them to someone whom he had absolutely determined never to pardon.

Even the fear of having committed this sin can be a hopeful sign that the fearful person has not committed it.

A trembling, contrite sinner has this witness within.

Words reveal what fills the heart (verses 33–37)

Our speech reveals our character, just as an accent may reveal the country we come from.

The heart is the spring; our words are the streams.

If the source is polluted, its waters will also be polluted.

Only the grace of God, like salt used to heal a spring, can renew the heart, guide the tongue and cleanse corrupt conversation.

A wicked person's heart holds a store of evil desires.

From this store come words and deeds that dishonor God and injure neighbors.

We should continually watch ourselves, ensuring that our speech suits the character of a Christian.

The demand for a sign and the danger of empty reform (verses 38–45)

Christ welcomes holy desires and faithful prayers.

But those who ask with wrong motives may ask and receive nothing.

God gave signs to people such as Abraham and Gideon who wanted their faith strengthened, while refusing signs demanded as an excuse for unbelief.

The great proof that Christ is Messiah is his resurrection from the dead by his own power, the sign of Jonah.

As Jonah was preserved for three days and nights in the great fish and then emerged alive, so Jesus would be in the grave and then rise.

The repentant Ninevites would shame those who refused repentance.

The queen of Sheba would shame those who refused to believe Christ, even though she had less light and greater difficulties.

Jesus' warning about the returning evil spirit pictures the condition of the Jewish church and nation.

It also applies to everyone who experiences some outward moral reform without genuine conversion.

An unclean spirit may leave a person's life temporarily.

If Christ does not dwell in the heart to keep it out, it finds a place cleaned by outward reform but still ready to obey sinful suggestions.

The person may become a stronger enemy of truth than before.

Every heart is a dwelling place of evil unless through faith in Christ it becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit.

Jesus identifies his true family (verses 46–50)

Christ taught clearly, familiarly and in ways his listeners could understand.

His mother and brothers were outside asking to speak with him, when it would have been better for them to be inside listening to his teaching.

Those closest to opportunities for grace often neglect them most, assuming they will always have another chance.

Yet tomorrow is not ours to command.

Friends and relatives may unintentionally interrupt our work or distract us with earthly concerns when our souls need attention.

Jesus was fully devoted to the work his Father gave him. Lesser duties did not lead him to neglect the greater.

This does not authorize disrespect toward parents or unkindness to relatives under the pretext of religion.

It means that lesser obligations must yield when a higher duty is presently required.

Let us cling to Christ and regard every genuine Christian, whatever that person's worldly station, as the brother, sister or mother of the Lord of glory.

Love, respect and serve them for his sake and after his example.

Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
Jesus defends his disciples for plucking corn on the sabbath day. | (1-8) |
Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the sabbath. | (9-13) |
The malice of the Pharisees. | (14-21) |
Jesus heals a demoniac. | (22-30) |
Blasphemy of the Pharisees. | (31-32) |
Evil words proceed from an evil heart. | (33-37) |

Verses 1-8
Being in the corn-fields, the disciples began to pluck the ears of corn: the law of God allowed it, [Deut.23.25] De 23:25. This was slender provision for Christ and his disciples; but they were content with it. The Pharisees did not quarrel with them for taking another man's corn, but for doing it on the sabbath day. Christ came to free his followers, not only from the corruptions of the Pharisees, but from their unscriptural rules, and justified what they did. The greatest shall not have their lusts indulged, but the meanest shall have their wants considered. Those labours are lawful on the sabbath day which are necessary, and sabbath rest is to froward, not to hinder sabbath worship. Needful provision for health and food is to be made; but when servants are kept at home, and families become a scene of hurry and confusion on the Lord's day, to furnish a feast for visitors, or for indulgence, the case is very different. Such things as these, and many others common among professors, are to be blamed. The resting on the sabbath was ordained for man's good, [Deut.5.14] De 5:14. No law must be understood so as to contradict its own end. And as Christ is the Lord of the sabbath, it is fit the day and the work of it should be dedicated to him.
[Matt.12.9-Matt.12.13]
Verses 9-13
Christ shows that works of mercy are lawful and proper to be done on the Lord's day. There are more ways of doing well upon sabbath days, than by the duties of worship: attending the sick, relieving the poor, helping those who need speedy relief, teaching the young to care for their souls; these are doing good: and these must be done from love and charity, with humility and self-denial, and shall be accepted, [Gen.4.7] Ge 4:7. This, like other cures which Christ wrought, had a spiritual meaning. By nature our hands are withered, and we are unable of ourselves to do any thing that is good. Christ only, by the power of his grace, cures us; he heals the withered hand by putting life into the dead soul, works in us both to will and to do: for, with the command, there is a promise of grace given by the word.
[Matt.12.14-Matt.12.21]
Verses 14-21
The Pharisees took counsel to find some accusation, that Jesus might be condemned to death. Aware of their design, as his time was not come, he retired from that place. Face does not more exactly answer to face in water, than the character of Christ drawn by the prophet, to his temper and conduct as described by the evangelists. Let us with cheerful confidence commit our souls to so kind and faithful a Friend. Far from breaking, he will strengthen the bruised reed; far from quenching the smoking flax, or wick nearly out, he will rather blow it up into a flame. Let us lay aside contentious and angry debates; let us receive one another as Christ receives us. And while encouraged by the gracious kindness of our Lord, we should pray that his Spirit may rest upon us, and make us able to copy his example.
[Matt.12.22-Matt.12.30]
Verses 22-30
A soul under Satan's power, and led captive by him, is blind in the things of God, and dumb at the throne of grace; sees nothing, and says nothing to the purpose. Satan blinds the eyes by unbelief, and seals up the lips from prayer. The more people magnified Christ, the more desirous the Pharisees were to vilify him. It was evident that if Satan aided Jesus in casting out devils, the kingdom of hell was divided against itself; how then could it stand! And if they said that Jesus cast out devils by the prince of the devils, they could not prove that their children cast them out by any other power. There are two great interests in the world; and when unclean spirits are cast out by the Holy Spirit, in the conversion of sinners to a life of faith and obedience, the kingdom of God is come unto us. All who do not aid or rejoice in such a change are against Christ.
[Matt.12.31-Matt.12.32]
Verses 31-32
Here is a gracious assurance of the pardon of all sin upon gospel terms. Christ herein has set an example to the sons of men, to be ready to forgive words spoken against them. But humble and conscientious believers, at times are tempted to think they have committed the unpardonable sin, while those who have come the nearest to it, seldom have any fear about it. We may be sure that those who indeed repent and believe the gospel, have not committed this sin, or any other of the same kind; for repentance and faith are the special gifts of God, which he would not bestow on any man, if he were determined never to pardon him; and those who fear they have committed this sin, give a good sign that they have not. The trembling, contrite sinner, has the witness in himself that this is not his case.
[Matt.12.33-Matt.12.37]
Verses 33-37
Men's language discovers what country they are of, likewise what manner of spirit they are of. The heart is the fountain, words are the streams. A troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring, must send forth muddy and unpleasant streams. Nothing but the salt of grace, cast into the spring, will heal the waters, season the speech, and purify the corrupt communication. An evil man has an evil treasure in his heart, and out of it brings forth evil things. Lusts and corruptions, dwelling and reigning in the heart, are an evil treasure, out of which the sinner brings forth bad words and actions, to dishonour God, and hurt others. Let us keep constant watch over ourselves, that we may speak words agreeable to the Christian character.
[Matt.12.38-Matt.12.45]
Verses 38-45
Though Christ is always ready to hear and answer holy desires and prayers, yet those who ask amiss, ask and have not. Signs were granted to those who desired them to confirm their faith, as Abraham and Gideon; but denied to those who demanded them to excuse their unbelief. The resurrection of Christ from the dead by his own power, called here the sign of the prophet Jonah, was the great proof of Christ's being the Messiah. As Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale, and then came out again alive, thus Christ would be so long in the grave, and then rise again. The Ninevites would shame the Jews for not repenting; the queen of Sheba, for not believing in Christ. And we have no such cares to hinder us, we come not to Christ upon such uncertainties. This parable represents the case of the Jewish church and nation. It is also applicable to all those who hear the word of God, and are in part reformed, but not truly converted. The unclean spirit leaves for a time, but when he returns, he finds Christ is not there to shut him out; the heart is swept by outward reformation, but garnished by preparation to comply with evil suggestions, and the man becomes a more decided enemy of the truth. Every heart is the residence of unclean spirits, except those which are temples of the Holy Ghost, by faith in Christ.
[Matt.12.46-Matt.12.50]
Verses 46-50
Christ's preaching was plain, easy, and familiar, and suited to his hearers. His mother and brethren stood without, desiring to speak with him, when they should have been standing within, desiring to hear him. Frequently, those who are nearest to the means of knowledge and grace are most negligent. We are apt to neglect that which we think we may have any day, forgetting that to-morrow is not ours. We often meet with hinderances in our work from friends about us, and are taken off by care for the things of this life, from the concerns of our souls. Christ was so intent on his work, that no natural or other duty took him from it. Not that, under pretence of religion, we may be disrespectful to parents, or unkind to relations; but the lesser duty must stand by, while the greater is done. Let us cease from men, and cleave to Christ; let us look upon every Christian, in whatever condition of life, as the brother, sister, or mother of the Lord of glory; let us love, respect, and be kind to them, for his sake, and after his example.

The parable of the sower (verses 1–23)

Jesus preached from a boat to avoid the crowd pressing too closely and to allow his voice to be heard.

This teaches us to use faithfully the practical arrangements Providence provides for worship, without seeking outward splendor.

Parables make divine truth clear to those willing to learn while leaving it obscure to those determined to remain ignorant.

The seed is God's word. Christ sows it, either personally or through his ministers.

Preaching to a crowd is like scattering grain: we cannot know where the seed will take root.

Four kinds of soil describe four responses of the heart.

The path represents careless hearers. Satan is both the great murderer of souls and the thief of sermons, stealing the word from those who neglect to keep it.

Rocky soil represents hypocrites who quickly display enthusiasm, sometimes exceeding the outward enthusiasm of genuine Christians.

They enjoy messages about free salvation, Christian privileges and heaven.

Yet without a changed heart, lasting conviction of sin, awareness of their need for a Savior or love for holiness, they claim assurance without foundation.

When persecution comes, or a tempting sinful advantage appears, they abandon or conceal their profession and seek an easier form of religion.

Thorny soil represents worldly cares.

Thorns came through sin and are part of the curse. They may serve a practical purpose, yet they entangle, hurt and eventually burn (Hebrews 6:8).

Worldly anxiety prevents us from benefiting from God's word.

The deceitfulness of riches harms us precisely when we trust wealth as a source of safety and happiness. It chokes the seed.

Good soil is marked by fruitfulness, which distinguishes genuine believers from hypocrites.

Christ does not say the good ground has no stone or thorn at all, only that nothing is allowed to destroy its fruit.

True believers differ in fruitfulness.

We should seek to bear the greatest possible harvest.

Hearing God's word is one of the best uses of our hearing. Let us examine ourselves: What kind of hearer am I?

The weeds among the wheat (verses 24–30 and 36–43)

The weeds picture the condition of Christ's church in this life and at the final judgment.

The parable describes Christ's care, the devil's hostility, good and bad mixed together now, and their final separation.

Sin grows readily in fallen humanity, just as weeds grow without tending.

Good seed requires care, watering and protection.

When the servants complained about weeds in a good field, their master had not caused the problem.

Whatever is wrong in Christ's church certainly does not originate with Christ.

Openly wicked people and those persistently opposing the gospel should not be treated as faithful church members.

Yet no human judgment can separate genuine believers from hypocrites perfectly.

Even opponents should be instructed with meekness, not destroyed as though we were authorized to carry out final judgment ourselves.

The great day will reveal clearly what is hard to discern in this world.

God's coming judgment should restrain us from wrongdoing.

At death believers will recognize their own heavenly glory; on judgment day they will shine before the whole world.

Their light is borrowed from the Fountain of light.

Then their sanctification will be perfected and their justification publicly made known.

May we be found among them.

The mustard seed and leaven (verses 31–35)

The gospel began in apparent smallness but would expand greatly.

So it is with God's grace in an individual heart. If grace is genuine, it grows even when its first beginnings are almost imperceptible.

Over time it becomes strong and useful.

The gospel also works like leaven, gradually but certainly transforming the heart.

May God give us faith to rely on his promise, making us willing for every service or sacrifice.

Jesus' final warning corrects another mistake.

The heavenly inheritance is not distributed like earthly inheritances, according to outward position or expectation.

It follows God's pleasure.

Do not trust outward profession or an appearance of future greatness.

Others who seem unlikely now may yet become distinguished in faith and holiness.

Verses 1-2
Great multitudes followed Christ. When Christ departs, it is best for us to follow him. They found him as able and ready to help elsewhere, as he had been in Galilee; wherever the Sun of Righteousness arose, it was with healing in his wings.
[Matt.19.3-Matt.19.12]
Verses 3-12
The Pharisees were desirous of drawing something from Jesus which they might represent as contrary to the law of Moses. Cases about marriage have been numerous, and sometimes perplexed; made so, not by the law of God, but by the lusts and follies of men; and often people fix what they will do, before they ask for advice. Jesus replied by asking whether they had not read the account of the creation, and the first example of marriage; thus pointing out that every departure therefrom was wrong. That condition is best for us, and to be chosen and kept to accordingly, which is best for our souls, and tends most to prepare us for, and preserve us to, the kingdom of heaven. When the gospel is really embraced, it makes men kind relatives and faithful friends; it teaches them to bear the burdens, and to bear with the infirmities of those with whom they are connected, to consider their peace and happiness more than their own. As to ungodly persons, it is proper that they should be restrained by laws, from breaking the peace of society. And we learn that the married state should be entered upon with great seriousness and earnest prayer.
[Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15]
Verses 13-15
It is well when we come to Christ ourselves, and bring our children. Little children may be brought to Christ as needing, and being capable of receiving blessings from him, and having an interest in his intercession. We can but beg a blessing for them: Christ only can command the blessing. It is well for us, that Christ has more love and tenderness in him than the best of his disciples have. And let us learn of him not to discountenance any willing, well-meaning souls, in their seeking after Christ, though they are but weak. Those who are given to Christ, as part of his purchase, he will in no wise cast out. Therefore he takes it ill of all who forbid, and try to shut out those whom he has received. And all Christians should bring their children to the Saviour that he may bless them with spiritual blessings.
[Matt.19.16-Matt.19.22]
Verses 16-22
Christ knew that covetousness was the sin which most easily beset this young man; though he had got honestly what he possessed, yet he could not cheerfully part with it, and by this his want of sincerity was shown. Christ's promises make his precepts easy, and his yoke pleasant and very comfortable; yet this promise was as much a trial of the young man's faith, as the precept was of his charity and contempt of the world. It is required of us in following Christ, that we duly attend his ordinances, strictly follow his pattern, and cheerfully submit to his disposals; and this from love to him, and in dependence on him. To sell all, and give to the poor, will not serve, but we are to follow Christ. The gospel is the only remedy for lost sinners. Many abstain from gross vices who do not attend to their obligations to God. Thousands of instances of disobedience in thought, word, and deed, are marked against them in the book of God. Thus numbers forsake Christ, loving this present world: they feel convictions and desires, but they depart sorrowful, perhaps trembling. It behoves us to try ourselves in these matters, for the Lord will try us.
[Matt.19.23-Matt.19.30]
Verses 23-30
Though Christ spoke so strongly, few that have riches do not trust in them. How few that are poor are not tempted to envy! But men's earnestness in this matter is like their toiling to build a high wall to shut themselves and their children out of heaven. It should be satisfaction to those who are in a low condition, that they are not exposed to the temptations of a high and prosperous condition. If they live more hardly in this world than the rich, yet, if they get more easily to a better world, they have no reason to complain. Christ's words show that it is hard for a rich man to be a good Christian, and to be saved. The way to heaven is a narrow way to all, and the gate that leads into it, a strait gate; particularly so to rich people. More duties are expected from them than from others, and more sins easily beset them. It is hard not to be charmed with a smiling world. Rich people have a great account to make up for their opportunities above others. It is utterly impossible for a man that sets his heart upon his riches, to get to heaven. Christ used an expression, denoting a difficulty altogether unconquerable by the power of man. Nothing less than the almighty grace of God will enable a rich man to get over this difficulty. Who then can be saved? If riches hinder rich people, are not pride and sinful lusts found in those not rich, and as dangerous to them? Who can be saved? say the disciples. None, saith Christ, by any created power. The beginning, progress, and perfecting the work of salvation, depend wholly on the almighty power of God, to which all things are possible. Not that rich people can be saved in their worldliness, but that they should be saved from it. Peter said, We have forsaken all. Alas! it was but a poor all, only a few boats and nets; yet observe how Peter speaks, as if it had been some mighty thing. We are too apt to make the most of our services and sufferings, our expenses and losses, for Christ. However, Christ does not upbraid them; though it was but little that they had forsaken, yet it was their all, and as dear to them as if it had been more. Christ took it kindly that they left it to follow him; he accepts according to what a man hath. Our Lord's promise to the apostles is, that when the Son of man shall sit on the throne of his glory, he will make all things new, and they shall sit with him in judgement on those who will be judged according to their doctrine. This sets forth the honour, dignity, and authority of their office and ministry. Our Lord added, that every one who had forsaken possessions or comforts, for his sake and the gospel, would be recompensed at last. May God give us faith to rest our hope on this his promise; then we shall be ready for every service or sacrifice. Our Saviour, in the last verse, does away a mistake of some. The heavenly inheritance is not given as earthly ones are, but according to God's pleasure. Let us not trust in promising appearances or outward profession. Others may, for aught we know, become eminent in faith and holiness.

Third, the final reward of the saints is not measured by how long ago they were converted.

The parable describes the visible church and explains different ways in which the last become first and the first last.

Until God calls us to his work, we remain idle all day.

A sinful life is actually hard service to Satan, yet it is idleness with respect to God.

The marketplace represents the world, from which the gospel summons us.

Come away from the marketplace and serve God.

His work does not allow carelessness.

A person may drift into destruction through idleness, but the path to heaven requires diligence.

The Roman denarius, the coin paid for the day's work, is explained by Henry using a value in the currency of his own time (seven and a half old English pence), as sufficient wages then for a day's support; that historical comparison is not a modern wage conversion.

This reward does not mean obedience creates a debt God must pay.

After all our service, we are still unprofitable servants.

Nevertheless, God sets an actual reward before his people.

The eleventh-hour call is no excuse to postpone repentance until old age.

The late workers had not earlier received an offer of work.

Similarly, the Gentiles were called when the gospel first reached them.

Those who have already heard repeated gospel invitations and refused them will not be able to claim later that no one called them.

Do not be discouraged, but do not delay.

Now is the accepted time.

Proud Pharisees and merely nominal Christians often complain when God's grace is generous to others.

We tend to imagine that God has favored others too much and us too little, or that we have worked far harder than others.

But God's kindness to another person is no injustice to us.

Worldly people choose their payment in this present life.

Believers must remember that they seek heaven as their inheritance.

Why then should they expect ultimate satisfaction from earthly goods?

God punishes no one beyond what is deserved and never neglects faithful service.

By showing extraordinary grace to some, he wrongs no one.

Envy is an evil eye: resenting someone else's happiness and desiring harm for them.

It pains the envious person, displeases God and hurts neighbors.

It brings neither real pleasure, profit nor honor.

Let us abandon claims of merit and seek salvation as a free gift.

Rather than begrudging divine mercy, rejoice when God shows it to others.

Jesus predicts his suffering and resurrection (verses 17–19)

Jesus now spoke even more specifically about his approaching suffering.

As before, he also promised his resurrection and glory, encouraging and comforting the disciples.

Seeing by faith the Savior who was once crucified and is now glorified humbles proud and self-justifying hearts.

When we recognize that the Son of God needed to be humbled and suffer for the salvation of sinners, we understand more clearly the freedom and abundance of grace.

Jesus answers the ambition of James and John (verses 20–28)

The sons of Zebedee misused Christ's promise of future comfort as an opportunity for personal ambition.

Some people take even spiritual encouragement and turn it toward selfish purposes.

Pride easily besets us.

Seeking to surpass others in rank and splendor is sinful ambition.

Jesus corrected their request by speaking of the suffering his followers would endure.

Their cup could be bitter and cause trembling, yet it was not the cup of God's wrath against the wicked.

It was a cup held by their Father (John 18:11).

Suffering may be severe but it is temporary—a cup that will eventually be emptied.

Henry likens suffering for Christ to baptism, which signifies joining the Lord in covenant and fellowship.

He describes baptism as an outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace, and sees sufferings in Christ's service as signs of that grace too (Ezekiel 20:37; Isaiah 48:10; Philippians 1:29).

James and John did not yet understand the full meaning of Christ's cup or baptism.

Often those who speak most confidently know least about the cross.

Ambition causes profound damage among brothers and sisters.

Wherever the disciples quarreled, the desire for greatness lay beneath it.

The one who serves most diligently, suffers most patiently, seeks the good of fellow believers and labors for the salvation of souls resembles Christ most closely.

Such a servant will receive the greatest honor from Christ in eternity.

Jesus described his own death using the language of Old Testament sacrifices.

His sacrifice for human sin is the true and substantial offering, of which the legal sacrifices were only faint and incomplete pictures.

He gave his life as a ransom for many: a sacrifice sufficient for all, effective in many.

A trembling believer may therefore ask, “Why not for me?”

People sharing the same illness or trial do well to pray together, encouraging one another.

Christ has mercy enough for everyone who asks him.

The blind men prayed earnestly. They cried as people who genuinely desired help.

Cold, indifferent desires are unlikely to obtain what is needed.

They prayed humbly, placing themselves in the hands of the merciful Mediator.

Henry attributes this confession to the Holy Spirit.

They also persevered, refusing to fall silent when others discouraged them.

Jesus received and encouraged them.

Till we are hired into the service of God, we are standing all the day idle: a sinful state, though a state of drudgery to Satan, may be called a state of idleness. The market-place is the world, and from that we are called by the gospel. Come, come from this market-place. Work for God will not admit of trifling. A man may go idle to hell, but he that will go to heaven, must be diligent. The Roman penny was sevenpence halfpenny in our money, wages then enough for the day's support. This does not prove that the reward of our obedience to God is of works, or of debt; when we have done all, we are unprofitable servants; but it signifies that there is a reward set before us, yet let none, upon this presumption, put off repentance till they are old. Some were sent into the vineyard at the eleventh hour; but nobody had hired them before. The Gentiles came in at the eleventh hour; the gospel had not been before preached to them. Those that have had gospel offers made them at the third or sixth hour, and have refused them, will not have to say at the eleventh hour, as these had, No man has hired us. Therefore, not to discourage any, but to awaken all, be it remembered, that now is the accepted time. The riches of Divine grace are loudly murmured at, among proud Pharisees and nominal Christians. Obedient believers agree with God for their penny in the other world, and must remember they have so agreed. Didst not thou agree to take up with heaven as thy portion, thy all; wilt thou seek for happiness in the creature? God punishes none more than they deserve, and recompenses every service done for him; he therefore does no wrong to any, by showing extraordinary grace to some. See here the nature of envy. It is an evil eye, which is displeased at the good of others, and desires their hurt. It is a grief to ourselves, displeasing to God, and hurtful to our neighbours: it is a sin that has neither pleasure, profit, nor honour.
